Penelope. The faithful wife of Odysseus who waited twenty years for her husband's return from the Trojan War, celebrated for her constancy and her clever resistance to suitors.

Penelope was the wife of Odysseus, king of Ithaca, and mother to Telemachus. A princess of Sparta by birth, she became queen of Ithaca. When Odysseus sailed for Troy, she was left alone to rule the kingdom. She endured a decade of war waiting for him to return, but he did not come home when the fighting ended.

More than a hundred noble suitors descended on Ithaca, demanding she marry one of them. They consumed her household's resources and tested her patience day after day. Famously, she wove a burial shroud for her father-in-law by day and unraveled it by night, buying years of time without choosing a husband. She remained utterly faithful to Odysseus despite his decade-long absence after the war, sustained only by rumors and hope.

Through her wit and constancy, Penelope preserved her son's inheritance and her own honor against impossible pressure. Eventually, after twenty years of separation, Odysseus returned home. He slew the suitors who had invaded their kingdom, and Penelope and Odysseus were reunited. Their marriage and kingdom were restored after two decades apart. She was bound to Odysseus, her husband whose long journey home she faithfully awaited. Telemachus, their son, came of age during his father's absence and sought news of him. The Odyssey, the epic that tells her patient vigil, immortalized her steadfast hope.
